flashcards.q: Define covariate shift, prior/label shift, and concept drift precisely.
flashcards.a: Covariate shift: P(X) changes, P(Y|X) fixed. Prior/label shift: P(Y) changes, P(X|Y) fixed. Concept drift: P(Y|X) itself changes — the model's learned relationship is no longer true.

flashcards.q: Which type of shift necessarily degrades accuracy, and why do the others not?
flashcards.a: Only concept drift necessarily degrades accuracy, because it changes the actual relationship the model learned. Covariate and label shift can leave a well-generalizing model just as accurate on the new distribution/class balance.

flashcards.q: State PSI's formula and standard action thresholds.
flashcards.a: PSI = Σ(cur%-ref%)·ln(cur%/ref%) over buckets (typically 10, from reference-distribution deciles). <0.10 no significant shift; 0.10-0.25 investigate; ≥0.25 significant shift, action needed. A banking-industry convention, not derived from first principles.

flashcards.q: Why must PSI buckets be built from the reference distribution's quantiles, not the current distribution's?
flashcards.a: Bucketing on the reference distribution means each bucket starts with an even split (e.g. 10% each) by construction, so any departure in the current distribution is the real drift signal. Bucketing on current data instead makes it always look artificially uniform against itself.

flashcards.q: Why does the KS test's p-value become useless at large sample sizes?
flashcards.a: Statistical power scales with n; at production scale (10^5+ samples), even a trivial, practically meaningless difference produces a near-zero p-value. Fix: threshold the KS statistic (max CDF distance, a real effect size) instead of the p-value, or fix the sample size before testing.

flashcards.q: Contrast KL divergence, JS divergence, and Wasserstein distance.
flashcards.a: KL: asymmetric, undefined where reference has zero probability but current doesn't (breaks on sparse categoricals). JS: symmetrized, bounded [0,1], always finite. Wasserstein: respects actual numeric distance between values, not just bucket-proportion shape — correctly distinguishes 'mass moved a little' from 'mass moved a lot.'

flashcards.q: How does a domain classifier detect multivariate drift that univariate tests miss?
flashcards.a: Label reference-window rows 0 and current-window rows 1, train a classifier to distinguish them on the full feature set. AUC ≈ 0.5 means no detectable joint drift; AUC ≥ ~0.7 means a real, learnable difference exists even if every individual feature's marginal test passed.

flashcards.q: Why does a rolling reference window hide slow, gradual drift?
flashcards.a: If each window is compared only to the window right before it, drift slower than the window length looks like a series of insignificant changes even though cumulative drift from the original training distribution can be enormous — the reference itself drifts along with the data.

flashcards.q: What's the fix for the rolling-reference blind spot to slow drift?
flashcards.a: Keep a frozen training-time reference for long-horizon cumulative drift detection alongside a rolling short window for fast operational alerting — they answer different questions and neither substitutes for the other.

flashcards.q: Name the three retraining trigger types and the failure mode of using each alone.
flashcards.a: Scheduled (wastes compute on stable periods, misses fast drift between runs). Threshold-based (retrains on statistical noise or benign shift that doesn't hurt accuracy). Performance-based (never fires in time without fast labels or a trustworthy estimation method). Mature practice combines all three: scheduled floor, drift gate, performance corroboration.

flashcards.q: What does CBPE-style performance estimation (e.g. NannyML) do and why does it matter?
flashcards.a: Estimates a model's accuracy/AUC on unlabeled production data from its own confidence outputs plus observed drift, calibrated against labeled validation data. It matters because it closes the gap between 'drift detected' and 'did performance actually drop,' the thing drift alone can't answer.

flashcards.q: Distinguish sudden, gradual, incremental, and recurring/seasonal drift.
flashcards.a: Sudden: step function (pipeline/schema change). Gradual: slow monotonic trend (evolving user behavior). Incremental: many small changes accumulating noisily. Recurring/seasonal: cyclical (weekday/weekend, holidays) — often better addressed by a season-aware model than by retraining.

flashcards.q: Why is 'drift detected' not the same claim as 'model broken'?
flashcards.a: Drift only measures that a distribution changed; only concept drift is guaranteed to hurt accuracy. Covariate/label shift can be detected with high PSI while the business metric and accuracy stay completely flat — retraining on that signal alone wastes compute.
